headline: Hot Inflation and Weak Bond Sales Push Rates to 7.42%
tileReason: A hotter inflation report, two weak government bond sales and a near-certain December Fed hike pushed the daily 30-year average up 0.25% this week.
takeaway:
Rates gave back a month of progress in three trading days. The daily 30-year average started the week at 7.17%, its lowest since late September, and finished Thursday at 7.42%, up 0.25% and the highest since early October. Friday's index had not posted when this was written. Freddie Mac's weekly survey fell to 7.11%, but it mostly reflects quotes gathered before this week's jump, so it lags what borrowers are seeing now.

Tuesday's inflation report did the most damage. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October versus 0.3% expected, and core prices, which leave out food and energy, rose 0.3% versus 0.2%. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, rose from 4.86% at last Friday's close to 5.10% Thursday, and news reports put its weekly climb among the biggest since April 2025.

Weak bond sales piled on. The Treasury's 10-year sale Tuesday and 30-year sale Thursday both drew soft demand, so the government had to pay slightly higher yields than the market expected to sell all that debt. Oil gave little help: it fell below $90 a barrel early in the week on Iran talk hopes, then bounced back as talks stalled. Friday's wholesale inflation report rose 0.3% versus 0.4% expected, a bit milder than feared, but the 10-year yield was still trading around 5.15% Friday.

Lenders absorbed part of the selloff. Mortgage rates rose about the same as the 10-year yield this week, but they still sit unusually far above it: the Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, was about 2.17% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 9, versus a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra cushion is room for mortgage rates to improve if markets calm down.

A December Fed hike now looks close to certain. Futures markets put the odds of a Dec 9 hike at about 78% to 81% on Monday; by Friday, sources showed roughly 85% to 91% for a quarter-point hike with the rest on a bigger half-point move, so a hike of some size is close to fully priced. Governor Christopher Waller floated a half-point move, and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan and other officials said more increases look appropriate.

So far, Monday's 30-day outlook leaned toward rates staying about where they were, and they have moved higher instead. That call is graded Dec 9. Next week's tests: October retail sales and Nvidia's earnings Tuesday, the minutes of the Fed's October meeting Wednesday, and weekly jobless claims Thursday.

drivers.title: October inflation runs hotter than forecast
drivers.text: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October versus 0.3% expected, and core prices rose 0.3% versus 0.2%. Hotter inflation makes bond investors demand higher yields and makes more Fed hikes likely, so the 10-year yield jumped about 0.10% Tuesday alone and the daily mortgage average rose 0.12%.

drivers.title: Fed hike bets firm up
drivers.text: Odds of a Dec 9 hike climbed from about 78%-81% on Monday to near-certain by midweek, with a small chance of a half-point move, as Waller, Logan, Goolsbee and other officials talked up more increases. Markets also began pricing another hike early next year. Expected higher short-term rates pull longer-term rates, including mortgages, up with them.

drivers.title: Weak demand at the 10- and 30-year bond sales
drivers.text: Tuesday's $42 billion 10-year sale drew its softest demand since May, and Thursday's $25 billion 30-year sale also went at a slightly higher yield than expected. When buyers need extra yield to absorb new government debt, long-term yields rise, and mortgage rates rose another 0.12% Thursday.

drivers.title: Oil swings on Iran headlines
drivers.text: Brent crude briefly fell below $90 a barrel Tuesday for the first time since August, which helped early in the week, then rebounded toward the mid-$90s as Iran talks stalled. The rebound added to inflation worries in the second half of the week.

drivers.title: Milder wholesale prices and a wide lender cushion
drivers.text: Friday's producer price report rose 0.3% versus 0.4% expected, trimming the odds of a half-point Fed move, and mortgage rates still sit about 2.17% above the 10-year yield versus a 1.76% long-run average. Both gave borrowers a little support, though not enough to offset the week's selloff.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average climbed from 7.17% to 7.42% this week, erasing most of October's improvement, though it's still below the 7.6%-plus levels of early October. Each 0.25% adds roughly $50 a month per $300,000 borrowed. If you're under contract or close, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates fall after you lock) or waiting would each fit your timeline.
talkingPoints.sellers: Buyers felt this week's jump, and October existing home sales fell 5.5%. With a December Fed hike widely expected, sharp pricing or a seller credit that helps a buyer lower their rate can keep a listing competitive.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates jumped from about 7.17% to 7.42% this week as hot inflation, weak government bond sales and a near-certain December Fed hike pushed the 10-year Treasury yield above 5%.
